title: Maximise Upper-Left Submatrix Sum
statement:
You are given a `2N x 2N` matrix of integers. You may perform the following operation any number of times, in any order: choose one row **or** one column and **reverse** it (the first element swaps with the last, the second with the second last, and so on).

After performing any sequence of such operations (including none), look at the upper-left `N x N` submatrix, which consists of the cells in rows `0` to `N - 1` and columns `0` to `N - 1`. Find the **maximum possible sum** of the elements of that submatrix.

Values may be negative.
inputFormat:
The first line contains the integer `N`.
Each of the next `2N` lines contains `2N` integers: one row of the matrix.
outputFormat: Print one integer: the maximum possible sum of the upper-left `N x N` submatrix.

examples.explanation: N = 1, so the upper-left submatrix is a single cell. Reversing a row or column can bring any of the four values into that cell; the best is 4.

Each upper-left cell can be filled with the largest of the four cells that mirror it: (0,0) from {112, 119, 62, 108} gives 119; (0,1) from {42, 83, 98, 114} gives 114; (1,0) from {56, 49, 15, 43} gives 56; (1,1) from {125, 56, 78, 101} gives 125. The sum is 119 + 114 + 56 + 125 = 414.
All values are negative; the best cell value is -1.

hints: Try N = 1 and N = 2 by hand. For a cell (i, j) in the upper-left block, which other cells of the whole matrix could be moved into that position?
Reversing row i swaps (i, j) with (i, 2N-1-j); reversing column j swaps (i, j) with (2N-1-i, j). So every cell belongs to a group of four mirror-image cells.
It turns out that each upper-left cell can independently receive the maximum of its group of four. Sum those maxima, and be ready to justify why the choices do not conflict.
